title: Keep your word, set team standards and plan your next 90 days

say: Keep your word, set team standards, and plan your next 90 days.
This is the video for module four of Ethics and Accountability at Work.
Most trust at work is built or lost through ordinary promises. Vague promises like I'll look into it, or ready soon, are hard to keep and easy to argue about later.

panel.heading: Vague promise or clear commitment?
left: The dress will be ready soon.
right: Figures on WhatsApp by 4 pm tomorrow
At the shop by 7:45 to open at 8

say: A clear commitment says what exactly, by when, and how the other person will know. I'll send the figures on WhatsApp by 4 pm tomorrow.
Keep all your promises on one list, with the person and the deadline, and check it every morning and evening. Look at it before you say yes to anything new.

panel.heading: Vague promise or clear commitment?
left: The dress will be ready soon.
right: Figures on WhatsApp by 4 pm tomorrow
At the shop by 7:45 to open at 8

say: For example, Kemi runs a tailoring business in Ilorin. On Monday she promised five aso-ebi dresses by Friday 5 pm, for a Saturday wedding.
On Wednesday her machine motor breaks. Two dresses are done, three still need about 9 hours of sewing, and the repair is only promised for Thursday afternoon.
That same Wednesday, she messages the customer and explains the situation briefly and honestly.
She offers an alternative: if the repair is late, she will pay a nearby tailor to sew from her cut pieces, at her own cost. And she promises an update on Thursday by 6 pm.
The repair is late, so she keeps her backup plan and checks every dress herself. All five are delivered at 4 pm on Friday. A late warning is far better than a missed deadline discovered by surprise.

panel.heading: Kemi renegotiates early
panel.rule: Tell them as soon as you know. Never go silent.

say: Groups need shared standards, so nobody has to rely only on personal courage. For example, Blessing owns a salon in Lagos. One evening the till was 8,000 naira short, and a staff member had used a customer's number to send personal messages.
In a 30-minute staff meeting, the team listed their risks and ranked the ones that were most likely and most harmful.

panel.heading: Blessing's salon puts controls in place

cards.d: The cashier and one stylist count at closing, and both sign.
No service is marked paid until the transfer reflects in the salon's account.
The booking book stays at the front desk. Numbers are used only for appointments.

say: First control: at closing, the cashier and one stylist count the till together, and both sign.

say: A short code that members helped to write is more useful than a long document nobody reads. Blessing's team wrote one page, read it together, and each person signed a copy.

panel.heading: A one-page code covers
items: Honesty in money, stock and attendance
Respect, and a safe way to speak up
Same consequences for leaders and members

say: Cover honesty in records, conflicts of interest and gifts, and how money is approved and reconciled.

panel.heading: A one-page code covers

Respect, and a safe way to speak up

say: Cover confidentiality, respect, and the right to raise a concern in good faith without punishment.

say: And apply the rules the same way to leaders and members. Introduce the code as protection for honest people, not an accusation. People watch what leaders do more than what they say.

say: Your capstone asks for an honest reflection. For example, Rukayat works at the front desk of a clinic in Abeokuta. A caller claimed to be family and asked about a patient.

panel.heading: Rukayat looks back honestly
items: The course tool that would have helped

say: Her values were in conflict: politeness and helpfulness against confidentiality.

panel.heading: Rukayat looks back honestly
items: The course tool that would have helped

say: She was busy, and gave a general answer before checking who was calling.

panel.heading: Rukayat looks back honestly
items: The course tool that would have helped

say: The patient later complained that a neighbour, not a relative, had learned private information.

panel.heading: Rukayat looks back honestly
items: The course tool that would have helped

say: Looking back, the personal data checklist would have stopped her.

panel.heading: Rukayat looks back honestly
items: The course tool that would have helped

say: Now she says: for privacy, I can't share patient information by phone. Honest reflection on a choice you regret often teaches the most.

panel.heading: Rukayat looks back honestly
items: The course tool that would have helped
panel.rule: Verify identity and consent before sharing patient information.

say: Turn your main lesson into one habit. Be more honest, or be on time, cannot be tracked.

panel.heading: Make the habit specific
right: A receipt for every payment I collect
Review my shared sheets every Friday

say: Give a receipt for every payment I collect, checked weekly. Arrive by 7:50 every working day, recorded in my notebook. Those you can count.
Rukayat ticks her notebook every shift for 90 days, with check-ins at days 30, 60 and 90. One habit kept is worth more than five abandoned in the second week.

say: Your practice. Track every promise you make for one week. Draft a one-page code for your team or group, and share it with one member.
Write your one-page reflection, remove identifying details, and set reminders for your day 30, 60 and 90 check-ins. Now continue with the lessons below.
